cur:catacombs-arles-concordius.summary: Under a lid carved with small scenes and an inscription, Christ sits enthroned at the centre of an arcaded colonnade, surrounded by the apostles seated in pairs on either side. The ordered, symmetrical composition presents Christ as the heavenly ruler and teacher of the apostolic college.
facts: The museum dates it to 380/390; it is carved from Carrara marble.
Commons has a separate photograph of the inscription on its lid, from which the sarcophagus takes the name of Concordius.
cur:catacombs-arles-concordius.notes: The apostles are not individually identifiable in the photograph.

cur:catacombs-bargello-raising-of-lazaru.summary: Within a ring of gold triangles, Christ raises Lazarus beside a tree; the gold figures are partly obscured by corrosion. The scene of Lazarus, the most frequent Gospel miracle in catacomb art, made this an apt object to set beside a Christian grave.
facts: The Bargello catalogues it as Roman, about 350–400, showing the raising of Lazarus.
Such gold-glass medallions survive mostly because they were embedded in the plaster sealing catacomb tombs.
cur:catacombs-bargello-raising-of-lazaru.notes: Surface damage makes the details hard to read; the identification follows the museum.

cur:manuscripts-rossano-gethsemane.summary: Against a dark hillside under a band of blue night sky, two haloed figures in gold robes bow to the ground in prayer — generally understood as Christ shown twice, kneeling and then fully prostrate, in his agony on the Mount of Olives. The stark composition, almost empty of other detail, conveys the solitude of his prayer before the Passion. Four prophets stand below.
facts: The diocesan museum lists this scene as 'Christ in the Gethsemane', the last of the Passion-week pictures before the canon-table title page.
Showing Christ in successive postures within one frame is a common device of early narrative illumination.

links.label: Museo Diocesano e del Codex: the miniatures

cur:manuscripts-rossano-gethsemane.notes: The reading of the two haloed figures as Christ shown twice is the usual interpretation; the paint surface is worn.

cur:monumental-nereo-achilleo-transfigur.summary: At the top of the arch, Christ appears in a radiant mandorla on the mountain between Moses and Elijah, with the three apostles fallen at the edges; at the left the Annunciation and at the right the Virgin and Child enthroned complete the arch. Though much restored, it is one of the few surviving mosaics from the pontificate of Leo III, the pope who crowned Charlemagne.
facts: The arch mosaics, from the time of Leo III, show the Annunciation, the Transfiguration in a mandorla, and the Theotokos with the Child.
The relics of Nereus, Achilleus and Flavia Domitilla were brought to the church from the Catacomb of Domitilla.
cur:monumental-nereo-achilleo-transfigur.notes: Wikipedia variously dates the mosaics to the time of Leo III and to 'the 9th century'.
